newsitem.title: FRANCE: Saudi barley deal keeps grain market in suspense.
newsitem.headline: Saudi barley deal keeps grain market in suspense.

text.p: Saudi Arabia is keeping world grain markets in suspense over a $130 million barley purchase likely to make or break prices for the specialist grain over coming months, grain exporters said on Friday.

The world's largest oil producer, once the proud owner of almost limitless funds to buy grain for its desert-wandering animal herds, is feeling the pinch after the expense of the Gulf war and may postpone purchasing in the hope of weaker prices.
"The Saudi (farm) ministry is asking whether now is the right time to buy barley, when prices could fall later in the year," a senior European grain trader said.
At stake is a provisional purchase of 800,000 tonnes of barley arranged between Saudi Arabia, the world's largest importer of the grain for animal feed, and a cluster of multinational trading firms.
More than a week after the deal was said to be all but wrapped up, traders are waiting for confirmation and say the kingdom could cut its purchase by a quarter to 600,000 tonnes.

After riding a record bull market for grain in the past year, barley prices are now under pressure from big new crops in the northern hemisphere and have given up 25 percent of their value to some $140-150 per tonne in recent months.

Europe, the United States, Canada and the former East Bloc are all competing to sell barley to the kingdom, which despite budget constraints is still one of the most reliable cash buyers of grain in the Middle East, traders said.

Competition between exporters came to a head on Thursday when the European Union, the largest barley producer, agreed to drop its price for barley to $145 from $150 to allow traders to cover roughly a third of their contracts with the German crop.

But improved supplies of feed wheat, which is too poor for bread-making and competes with barley for animal feed, are straining barley prices and could leave an opening for other exporters when fresh harvests arrive in November, traders said.

The EU is anxious to keep the lion's share of the prized barley trade with Saudi Arabia and has signalled it is ready to sell more by releasing an extra 300,000 tonnes of barley from its stores in Germany, grain officials said.

It is worried that unless it wraps up the sale quickly, it could lose market share to its rival Canada and face a surplus, barely a year after seeing its stocks dwindle to historic lows, the officials said.
Traders said the EU barley crop, the world's largest, could rebound to 51 million tonnes this year from some 44 million tonnes in 1995, leaving at least four million spare for export.
Barley prices are at or below guaranteed support levels in some EU countries, raising the prospect of big sales to EU stores when the buying-in season starts from November.
Canada is expcted to grow at least another two million tonnes this year which will be ready for export in November.
Traders said Riyadh had bought 800,000 tonnes, a fifth of its annual consumption, for October arrival at $160, equating to some $142 per tonne in Europe once freight costs are deducted.
Canada could snap up 150,000 tonnes of the deal, the United States 50,000 and the EU and ex-USSR the rest, traders said.
But cancelling a quarter of the purchase could open up stiff price competition between the EU and Canada later this year.
